https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-mislead.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OD3x The graph shows significant inconsistencies, and its data source is unclear Image: x.com/tomaszdechovsky Advertisement After Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers operated by the Russian technology company Yandex , claims began circulating online that the strikes had disrupted or even halted the activity of Russian propaganda bots. These accounts are often accused of spreading disinformation or artificially amplifying content on social media. During the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also suggested that the attacks on Yandex data centers had disrupted bot activity, saying "there was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations [because] there were fewer bots." In response to BBC Verify , Zelenskyy's office said that, rather than referring to reduced bot activity, the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media." The office added that it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users. So far, however, there is no clear evidence linking the attacks to a decline in bot activity. According to Josef Holnburger, managing director of the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), there is currently "no decline in Russian disinformation activities that could be explained by the attack on Yandex data centers." CeMAS systematically monitors such campaigns. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the attacks on Yandex data centers disrupted Russian activity Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/AFP European lawmaker shares graph without evidence on X Nevertheless, a misleading graph has been circulated as supposed evidence. It was shared, for example, by Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský. His post was viewed more than four million times on X . He suggested that the graph might demonstrate a decline in "online activity around AfD," although he did not specify what kind of activity he meant. In reality, the graph most likely demonstrates nothing at all. The German-language graph is titled "Daily activity over 3 months." It appears to show activity remaining relatively stable before dropping sharply in early October, roughly coinciding with the attacks on Yandex data centers. However, nothing in the graph itself indicates that this relates to AfD -related online activity. No source and faulty scaling The same applies to the graph's underlying data. It is unclear which data were used. No source is provided, nor is there any explanation of the data collection process or calculation method for the alleged "activity," which initially ranges between 6,000 and 7,000 before falling below 3,000. Particularly striking is that the graph extends to October 15. Its final data point appears to correspond to October 14 – a date that was still in the future when the graph first appeared online on October 11. Data for a future date cannot exist. The graph also contains scaling errors on both the X and Y axes. For example, on the Y axis, the distance between 2,500 and 3,000 is smaller than the other 500-unit intervals. Because the Y-axis does not begin at zero, the decline is visually exaggerated. On the X-axis, equal periods of time are represented by unequal distances. It is also unclear which platforms were analyzed and how the variable "activity" was calculated. The absence of a known data source, the inaccurate scaling, and the inclusion of "future" values strongly suggest that this is not a meaningful graph based on factual data and sound statistical methods. AI involvement cannot be proven, but is possible It is unclear whether AI was used to create the graph. Given the errors and the apparent "hallucination" of presenting future data, AI involvement cannot be ruled out. Misleading and error-filled graphs, some of which may have been AI-generated, appear regularly. German public broadcaster BR's #Faktenfuchs team recently reported on one such graph that falsely depicted industrial production in Germany (article in German). False or fabricated graphs can lend credibility to unsupported claims. The identity of the graph's creator remains unknown. What do Cloudflare data actually show? Cloudflare data are also frequently cited in connection with claims of declining bot activity. However, according to CeMAS managing director Holnburger, there is a misunderstanding about what Cloudflare's report actually means. Cloudflare provides services to many websites that block traffic assessed as non-human. Automated web traffic is common and includes, for example, crawlers that check websites for freshly published content. Search engines, including Yandex, rely on these crawlers. Other bots may be used for spam in comment sections. In a message to #Faktenfuchs, Holnburger writes, "a decline in bot activity on websites is something entirely different from a decline in inauthentic behavior by social bots on social networks." Referring to Cloudflare data , he added: "When looking at overall activity from Russian IP addresses on servers using Cloudflare services, there is no major decline in bot activity." Furthermore, there is no reason to assume that the infrastructure used by disinformation-related social bots would be hosted on Yandex data centers. "It is more likely that these systems are distributed across many different providers," Holnburger writes. The article was originally written in German and adapted into English by Alima de Graaf. This article is part of a collaboration between Germany's public broadcasting fact-checking teams ARD-Faktenfinder , BR24 #Faktenfuchs and DW Fact check . Ukraine attacks 'Russia's Google.' Photograph: Curt Anderson/AP View image in fullscreen Clouds hover over the entrance of the Florida state prison in Starke. Photograph: Curt Anderson/AP Florida Florida kills 77-year-old man in state’s 18th execution of year Vietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging halt Associated Press Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Florida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican governor Ron DeSantis’s aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term. William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a three-drug injection at Florida state prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River county deputy Richard Raczkowski. The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6pm execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he said: “No, I do not.” The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response. A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later. Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over the age of 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s ageing death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions. Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled. DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out. Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store. While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds. Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida supreme court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful. The US supreme court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment. The Florida supreme court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life. One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the department of corrections. The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the US Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves – an army veteran – as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam war. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution. A total of 47 people were executed in the US in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the US so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so. Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on 5 Novemner. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004. On August 11, France began requiring consumers' prior consent for sales calls. In Morocco, where French clients have long accounted for about 80% of call-center revenue, the government had warned that up to 50,000 jobs could be exposed, and a union federation estimates that about 10,000 may already have gone. The law was written for French consumers, not for Rabat. Casablanca felt it anyway. Morocco's Digital 2030 strategy calls for new markets. Central Europe, which made a similar journey over the past decade, has good reasons to pick up the phone. In 1960-61, Ahmed Cherkaoui, a young painter from Boujad who had studied in Paris, spent several months at the Academy of Fine Arts in Warsaw. He came on a Moroccan-Polish exchange, recommended by the UMT trade union. In Warsaw, he met the Polish avant-garde, above all Henryk Stażewski, pursued his experiments with burlap and mixed media, and in June 1961 showed his work at the Krzywe Koło gallery. In the summer of 1967, he left Paris for good, wanting to teach in Morocco and contribute to its development rather than chase fame abroad. He died in Casablanca that August, aged 32, already one of the pioneers of Moroccan modern painting. Six decades later, the road for Moroccan talent still runs mostly through Paris. Warsaw remains a rare and little-known stop.

The Paris pipeline

Moroccans are the largest group of foreign students in France: more than 42,000 in the 2024-2025 academic year, roughly one in ten international students, with 15% of them at engineering schools. In December 2022, former Higher Education Minister Abdellatif Miraoui said that around 700 doctors and between 2,000 and 3,000 engineers leave Morocco every year. Talk of the end of French influence would be premature. Paris announced in September 2021 that it would halve the number of visas issued to Moroccans, and restored normal consular relations only in December 2022. But French companies keep investing: the software group Cegid opened a center at Casablanca Finance City (CFC) in May and has hired 240 people there since June 2025. Paris has not lost its pull. It has stopped being enough.

One client, one law

Morocco's outsourcing sector employs about 150,000 people. In 2024, its digital and offshoring services exports reached MAD 26.2 billion, about $2.8 billion, according to the Exchange Office; IT services accounted for 40.3% of that and customer relations for 37.4%. Most of the sector's workers are in call centers, and call centers are the most exposed to France. Estimates vary: the government spoke of 40,000 to 50,000 jobs exposed to the law, the industry of no more than 10,000 directly at risk, and the UMT union reckons roughly that many may already have gone. Small call centers that lived on telemarketing have been hit hardest. Larger firms moved staff into customer service, back-office work and IT before the ban took effect, and Outsourcia has not closed a single site. What happens if the next rule from Paris covers technical support or IT services? And who replaces a French client that decides to cut costs? The targets of Digital Morocco 2030, MAD 40 billion in digital exports and 270,000 outsourcing jobs, will be hard to reach with one market and one foreign language. German firms have already come. Bertrandt and FEV, both automotive engineering companies, operate in Morocco, as does the engineering consultancy Fichtner, and call centers in Rabat, Tangier and Casablanca are hiring Dutch speakers. Polish technology companies are only beginning to look.

A Polish mirror

Poland and Morocco have almost the same population: 37.3 million and 36.8 million. In 2015, foreign-owned business service centers in Poland employed 150,000 people, roughly what Morocco's entire outsourcing sector employs today. A decade later, the sector accounts for close to half a million jobs and 6.1% of GDP, and its exports reached $48.4 billion in 2025, according to ABSL, the industry association. Poland did not build this on one client. Foreign-owned centers, led by American, British and German companies, account for 84% of the sector's jobs, and almost half of all centers work in IT. Their common working language is English. Consumer prices in Poland stand at 73% of the EU average, the third-lowest level in the Union, according to Eurostat. But Poland has its own problem. In 2017, 402,000 babies were born there; in 2025, about 238,000. A sector employing half a million people will have to find talent beyond its borders.

An office, not a consulate

That does not make Poland a second France for Moroccan graduates. The migration strategy Warsaw adopted in October 2024 promises a "selective model", tighter control of inflows and access to the labour market tied to the needs of the Polish economy. A country that loses thousands of engineers a year hardly needs another queue at another consulate. Central Europe's better offer is an office in Casablanca, Rabat or Tangier. Morocco has kept to UTC+1 since 2018, except during Ramadan, so Warsaw and Casablanca share a clock in winter and are an hour apart in summer. Paris has the same advantage; India, three and a half to four and a half hours ahead of Warsaw, does not. The groundwork exists. Poland's foreign ministry calls Morocco its leading partner on the African continent, and bilateral trade reached $2.5 billion in 2025, according to the Polish embassy in Rabat; in 2009 it was €180 million. In October 2025, Warsaw described Morocco's autonomy plan as "a serious, realistic, and pragmatic foundation for a lasting solution" to the Sahara dispute. The Polish Investment and Trade Agency has an office in Casablanca, and in December 2025, Asseco, Profil Software, INCAT and other Polish firms came to Casablanca Finance City for a Polish-Moroccan fintech conference. Polmlek, which bought the dairy company Jibal in 2022, employs about 1,500 people in Morocco. When the employers' confederation CGEM hosted Polish business leaders in Casablanca in November 2024, both sides spoke of Morocco as a gateway to Africa. A developer who writes code in Casablanca for a client in Warsaw does not show up in emigration statistics, and Morocco keeps the salary and the taxes. Cherkaoui needed a grant and a long journey to see what Warsaw had to offer. His successors need less: a Central European company willing to rent an office in Casablanca.
